newsitem.title: JAPAN: Fundamentals seen favouring weaker yen despite G7.
newsitem.headline: Fundamentals seen favouring weaker yen despite G7.

text.p: A call by world financial leaders for greater currency stability may do little to halt the yen's slide against the dollar given fundamental factors which point to a weaker Japanese currency, analysts said on Sunday.

Financial leaders from the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations said on Saturday that they were satisfied with a bounce back in the U.S. dollar from record lows hit two years ago, but avoided giving any clear new direction for the currency.

"We believe that major misalignments in exchange markets, noted in our April 1995 communique, have been corrected," said a statement issued after a one-day meeting of G7 finance ministers and central bankers in Berlin.

"We affirmed our views that exchange rates should reflect economic fundamentals and that excess volatility is undesirable. We agreed to monitor developments on the currency markets and to cooperate as necessary," the statement said.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka declared himself "quite satisfied" with the statement, saying it "made clear that the yen's downward correction process has been completely over."
The yen has fallen more than 50 percent against the dollar from its post-war high of 79.75 to the dollar in April 1995.

A weak yen boosts exports and thus helps Japan's economy, but Japanese authorities have campaigned for currency stability in fear that the yen's steep fall could cause the nation's trade surplus to balloon again and trigger an equally steep rise in the Japanese currency.
They have also feared a drastic yen decline would rattle Tokyo's already jittery stock market.

The G7 statement reflected a subtle change in Washington's strong dollar stance, one signalled on Friday when U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin jolted markets by hinting he might not be unhappy with some weakening of the U.S. currency.
Rubin reiterated his comments in Berlin on Saturday, repeating his mantra that a strong dollar was in U.S. interests, but adding, "We have had a strong dollar for some time now."
Analysts said it was tough to predict how Tokyo markets would react on Monday given currency gyrations in New York on Friday and a Japanese holiday on Tuesday.
The dollar, which had risen to a new four-year high of 124.72 yen, fell as low as 121.40 yen after Rubin's comments. But it pared the losses to end the day at around 123.13 yen.

"How is the market going to react? It boils down to what are central banks prepared to do -- whether they are prepared to spend money (to intervene) and to change interest rate policy," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at JP Morgan.
"From this communique, you get the sense that at this level, nobody is that concerned," he added.
Some analysts said the G7 statement might slow the pace of the yen's decline and one said it could prove a psychological turning point for the Japanese currency.
But most agreed that factors such as record low Japanese interest rates and worries over Japan's banking system's health meant there were few good reasons to buy yen.
"Since early January the pace of the yen's fall has picked up, so there might be some adjustment in the speed (of the decline)," said Akira Kurihara, a manager at Norinchukin Bank.
"But the fundamental trend is still toward a weaker yen, and it wouldn't be odd if it were to reach 130 to the dollar within the year," Kurihara added.

Rubin himself, in unusually blunt remarks in Berlin, voiced concern over Japan's economy and banking system. "They clearly have difficult issues to deal with," he said, adding, "these concerns merit a fair bit of attention going forward."

Japan has little scope for policies which might boost the yen given Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's commitment to fiscal tightening to address the nation's big budget deficit and the central bank's need to keep interest rates low to nurture the economy and soothe jitters over the banking system.

"Record low rates are going to stay with us and fiscal tightening is going ahead, so the fact that at current levels the G7 thinks everything is fine is not going to stop the markets from adjusting further," Koll said.
"Economic fundamentals point to further capital outflows from Japan and thus to yen depreciation."

With the G7 over, currency markets will look more closely at Japan's trade surplus for clues to when the yen will stop falling, analysts said. "The focus will be on how far the export-led recovery will come through in the data," Koll said.
